name: Felix Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business and finance at Ravenscar University, and I live at home above my dad's hardware store, Gupta & Son, on Station Road. Lectures are Monday to Thursday. Friday after class and all Saturday I'm behind the counter, and I also do the shop's online listings. I run most of my week through an AI assistant: summaries, spreadsheets, even product descriptions for the shop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What have you enjoyed most about your first term?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dad opened the store twenty years ago, and my mum does the books part-time. There's no spare money, and Dad doesn't pay me much, mostly pocket money and lunch. I got top results, and loans cover the fees. I believe in work and ownership. I'd like to build something of my own, and keep the shop going if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's possible, but it's already useful to me. If it only saves a bit of time, that's still a gain. I'd tell my friends not to wait for a revolution when there are small wins today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be worried, but about the shop. The big chains are cheaper and customers drift to them. Dad's margins are thin, and a bad year could close us. My own money is thin, too, with loans and about two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep making the shop's online presence better. I'd use the tools to write listings, answer customer messages and check stock. I'd try to bring in a few extra pounds a week by selling bulk orders to local builders. And I'd save every pound I could for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit pressured. I like the work, and I like being useful. But I don't enjoy seeing Dad's face when the till is quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad's shop competes with the big chains. What would a quiet future mean for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I use it all the time and it helps. If it fizzled, I'd lose some speed, but I'd still be fine. It's a tool, and a good one, but my future isn't built on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you be disappointed if it fizzled out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop might have to shrink to the best-selling lines, or move more online. I'd push Dad to do that earlier than he'd like. If it closed, I'd feel it as a family loss, not just a business one.

say: I'd say it's already **useful** to me, and small time savings are still a gain.
I'd tell friends not to wait for a revolution when there are **small wins** today.
think: I'd still worry, but about the **shop**: the big chains are cheaper and customers drift.
Dad's margins are thin, and a **bad year** could close us.
do: Improve the shop's **online presence** and use the tools for listings and stock checks.
Save every pound I can for a **rainy day**.
feel: Okay but a bit **pressured**: I don't enjoy seeing Dad's face when the till is quiet.
S0.quote: I don't enjoy seeing Dad's face when the till is quiet.
fieldNote: His anxiety is about the **family shop** and chain competition, not about AI.
Uses AI daily and sees it as a plain tool.
Prepared to push his father to move online sooner.

steps.text: Use AI to write the shop's online listings and answer messages
Sell bulk orders to local builders
Save twenty pounds a week for a rainy day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who move early. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and start something. Government should keep rules light, and let small businesses try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It worries me a bit for my degree, because finance is full of the tasks on the card: checking, planning, reports. But the same change makes it cheaper to start a business, so I'd rather be on the owner side than the employee side. That's a bet, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small online business on the side, maybe a store that sells tools and supplies to tradespeople, running with AI. I'd test it for a year while I keep my studies and my shop shifts. I'd put my profits into stock and an emergency fund. And I'd get a placement in a small finance firm to learn how money moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. And a bit nervous, because risk is risk. I like it when something is moving, and I'd rather act than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the thinking tasks on that card is the shop already handing to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stock ordering, product listings and customer questions. I use the tools for all three, and it cut my Saturday admin by a lot. That's about two hours saved, and I spend them calling customers instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pitch change to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Dad the numbers, not the buzzwords. I'd say, here's the hour it saved, and here's what we earn from the online sales. Dad trusts what he can count. If the numbers speak, he listens.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** for people who move early, and government should keep rules light.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools and **start something**.
think: Finance is full of **checking and planning**, so my degree is exposed.
The same change makes starting a business cheaper, so I'd rather be on the **owner side**.
do: Build a small online **business** selling supplies to tradespeople.
Test it for a year while I keep studying and **shop shifts**.
Get a **placement** in a small finance firm.
feel: **Excited**, with some nerves: I'd rather act than wait.
S1.quote: I'd show Dad the numbers, not the buzzwords. I'd say, here's the hour it saved, and here's what we earn from the online sales.
fieldNote: He wants to be **an owner**, and his optimism is about building.
The shop is a testing ground for the tools.
Traditional respect for his father shapes how he proposes change.

steps.text: Launch a small online supplies store for tradespeople
Use AI to cut Saturday stock admin at the shop
Apply for a placement at a small finance firm
Put the profits into stock and an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on to what's real: family, work, community. I'd tell people not to wait for the government, but to help each other. I'd say it online, and at our temple group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the degree is at risk, since finance is thinking work. I'd have debt and a market that doesn't need junior analysts. But the shop is hands-on, and robots come later. I'd feel that the shop might be safer than the degree, which is a strange thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work out how to use the two years. I'd put more hours into the shop and the online store, and learn everything I can about AI for small business. I'd keep my loan as low as I can. I'd also talk to Dad about the shop becoming the family's anchor while I try a few small ventures on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also a bit pumped. It's an odd mix. I'd probably have trouble sleeping, then wake up with a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is extremely fast. What do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first move more of the shop's sales online and set up automatic reordering. Then I'd ask a few builder customers for repeat contracts. If the two years go badly, we need cash in the bank, not stock on the shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Gupta & Son survive in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. The hands-on parts, like cutting keys and advising a customer who's fixing a leak, take longer for robots. The thinking parts, like ordering and pricing, change on the date. If we adapt the shop's thinking side early, we stay in the game.

say: I'd say hold on to what's real: **family, work, community**.
I'd tell people to help each other and not wait for the government.
think: The degree is at risk, since finance is **thinking work**, and I'd have debt.
The hands-on **shop** might be safer than my degree.
do: Put more hours into the **shop** and the online store.
Learn everything about **AI for small business**.
Talk to Dad about the shop being the family's **anchor**.
feel: **Scared** but a bit pumped: I'd have trouble sleeping, then wake up with a list.
S2.quote: The hands-on parts, like cutting keys and advising a customer who's fixing a leak, take longer for robots.
fieldNote: He sees the **shop as an anchor** and the degree as the shaky part.
Applies the card's three-year gap sensibly to hands-on and thinking work.
Fear and drive come together, which is typical of his adaptive style.

steps.text: Move more shop sales online and set up automatic reordering
Keep the loan as low as possible and build a cash reserve
Talk to Dad about making the shop the family anchor
Ask builder customers for repeat contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, so use it. Learn, build, save and take a few risks while the rules are still loose. I'd tell friends that the people who start now are the ones who'll be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better. I'd graduate in 2029, work for a couple of years, then start my own thing or take over part of the shop. I'd feel I can do something with five years. I'd rather be a founder than wait for a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a placement year at a small firm, then use savings to start an online business. I'd use the tools to run it on very little overhead. I'd keep a base of income from the shop, so that if my venture fails I'm not on the street. And I'd try to hire a friend, so we build it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with some fear. I like having five years. It's enough to try something, learn from it and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you in work for a couple of years before AGI. What would you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build first jobs for yourself. That's the core thing. If nobody hires you, hire yourself. It sounds rough, but it's also freeing. You decide what to do with the years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone scared of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get a skill, find a friend who's good at something else, and start. I'd also say talk to older people in your family. They've survived changes before, and they know that work and trust still count.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, so learn, build and save while rules are loose.
The people who start now are the ones who'll be ready.
think: I'd graduate in **2029**, work two years and then start my own thing.
I'd **rather be a founder** than wait for a job.
do: Finish the degree and take a **placement year** at a small firm.
Use savings to start an **online business** with very little overhead.
Keep a **base income** from the shop in case it fails.
feel: **Optimistic**, with some fear: five years is enough to try, learn and try again.
S3.quote: If nobody hires you, hire yourself. It sounds rough, but it's also freeing.
fieldNote: Five years turns him into **a builder**, and his plan is clear.
Keeps the shop as a safety net, a traditional family fallback.
His advice to others is practical and entrepreneurial.

steps.text: Take a placement year at a small finance firm
Start an online business with my savings after graduating
Keep a base income from shifts at the shop
Save five hundred pounds a term for the venture

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. We should build, trade and keep families together. I'd say the best thing governments can do is stay out of the way and keep training affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-eight. I might have a business running, or I might be managing the shop's second branch. I'd feel optimistic. Ten years is long enough to fail a few times and still be fine. The risk is getting comfortable, which I know I'm prone to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work somewhere for a year or two to learn how big companies think, then start my own business. I'd keep the shop alive, perhaps as a specialist for tradespeople, with AI handling the back office. I'd also save for my parents' retirement, and for a place of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Really good. This is the one where I think I can have what I want. Still some nerves, but they're the useful kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still take over the shop one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a changed form. The hands-on side stays, but ordering, pricing and customer messages would be done by software. Dad would stand at the counter and advise, and I'd run the system behind it. That seems fair, and it could keep us in business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a good outcome for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad and Mum retired comfortably, the shop still carrying our name and me with something of my own. A family that's still together on Sundays. That's what I'd want.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**: build, trade and keep families together.
Governments should stay out of the way and keep training **affordable**.
think: By twenty-eight I'd have **a business** running, or manage the shop's second branch.
The risk is getting **comfortable**, which I know I'm prone to.
do: Work a year or two at a **big company**, then start my own business.
Keep the shop alive as a **specialist** with AI handling the back office.
Save for my parents' **retirement** and a place of my own.
feel: **Really good**: the scenario where I think I can have what I want, with useful nerves.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to fail a few times and still be fine.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm**, and his plans for the shop and a business fit together.
His dad at the counter and him running the system is a neat picture of the family handover.
Admits being prone to comfort, a limit on his adaptiveness.

steps.text: Work at a big company for a year or two after graduating
Run the shop's ordering and pricing through AI software
Start my own business in my mid-twenties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the degree would be at risk before I've earned anything, and the shop would be asked to survive on its own. What would help is cheap loans for small business, simple training in how to use the tools and rules that keep big chains from squeezing small shops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that students like me aren't all scared. Some of us want to build things. But we need a fair rulebook and a bit of luck, and we need people to tell us the truth about what's coming.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be on the owner side than the employee side. That's a bet, though.
portrait: Felix is an **18-year-old** business and finance student who lives above his dad's hardware store and works there.
He uses AI **every day**, believes in work and ownership, and wants to build a business of his own.
He is **anxious** about the shop at first, uneasy as the AI case grows, and alarmed at two years.
With ten years he is **calm** and imagines running the shop's systems behind his dad.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario: his degree would be at risk before he has earned anything, and the shop would stand alone.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small business loans**, simple tool training, and rules that stop big chains squeezing small shops.
